◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Quantum computing harnesses superposition and entanglement to tackle problems impossible for classical computers — drug discovery, cryptography, optimization, and materials design. It is one of the most active frontiers in science and technology, turning quantum weirdness into raw computational power.

A qubit is the quantum version of a bit. Where a classical bit is strictly 0 or 1, a qubit can be in a superposition of both — and entangling many qubits unlocks a vast computational space.

The Qubit

Qubit
A qubit can be in state 0, state 1, or any superposition of both at once. Only when measured does it yield a definite 0 or 1, with probabilities set by the superposition.
Exponential state space
Thanks to superposition, n qubits represent 2ⁿ states simultaneously. Just 300 qubits could encode more states than there are atoms in the observable universe — the source of quantum computing's power.
🧠 ANALOGY

A classical bit is a coin lying flat — heads or tails. A qubit is a spinning coin — both at once until it lands. Many spinning coins, entangled together, let a quantum computer explore an enormous number of combinations in parallel, rather than checking them one at a time.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — how many states?
How many distinct states can 3 qubits represent simultaneously?
1
n qubits represent 2ⁿ states.
2
2³ = 8.
3 qubits can represent 8 states at once (000 through 111).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. How many states can 4 qubits represent simultaneously? (Use 2ⁿ.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

2ⁿ = 2⁴ = 16.

16 states
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. What is the key difference between a classical bit and a qubit? Explain below.
Show worked solution

A classical bit is always exactly 0 or 1. A qubit can be in a superposition of both 0 and 1 simultaneously, collapsing to a definite value only when measured.

A bit is 0 or 1; a qubit can be both at once (superposition)
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 3. How many states can 10 qubits represent at once? (2¹⁰.) Work below.
Show worked solution

2¹⁰ = 1024 states.

1024 states
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

A quantum computer doesn't simply "try all answers at once and read them off." Measurement collapses the qubits to a single result, so clever quantum algorithms are needed to make the right answer emerge with high probability. Qubits are also fragile — they lose their quantum state easily (decoherence), the central engineering challenge.

Key Takeaways
  • A qubit can be 0, 1, or a superposition of both.
  • n qubits represent 2ⁿ states simultaneously.
  • Superposition + entanglement give quantum computers their power.
  • Clever algorithms are needed; decoherence is the key challenge.
📊 FIGURE — the two headline algorithms
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — How big the speedups actually are

Grover’s algorithm searches an unstructured list — one with no index and no ordering — in roughly √N steps, where a classical scan needs about N/2 checks on average.

N = 1,000,000 Grover: sqrt(N) = 1000 steps classical: N/2 = 500000 checks ratio: 500x
computed with NumPy 2.4.6

A million-item list drops from about half a million checks to about 1000. Scale it to a trillion items and Grover needs about a million steps — still √N.

Shor’s algorithm is the other famous one, and it is a different class of win entirely: it factors large integers exponentially faster than any known classical method. That is the result that threatens RSA encryption, whose security rests on factoring being hard.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Filing both under "exponentially faster". Only Shor is exponential. Grover is quadratic — a real and useful speedup, but 500× on a million items, not astronomical. Doubling a Grover search only costs √2 more steps, so the gain grows slowly.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Remember them by what they attack: Shor → factoring → breaks encryption (exponential); Grover → searching → √N (quadratic).

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The measurement problem is quantum mechanics' deepest puzzle: why does a system in many states at once "collapse" to a single outcome when observed? The competing interpretations grapple with what quantum mechanics really says about reality — physics meeting philosophy.

Before measurement, a quantum system can exist in a superposition of many states at once. Measurement yields just one outcome — and why and how that happens is the famous measurement problem, with several competing interpretations.

Superposition and Collapse

Superposition
A quantum system can be in a combination of multiple states simultaneously — not "either/or" but "both at once," with each possibility weighted in the wavefunction.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
Measurement (collapse)
Upon measurement, the system yields a single definite result, and the wavefunction appears to collapse to that outcome. The probability of each result is given by |ψ|².
🧠 ANALOGY

Schrödinger's famous cat is in a superposition of "alive" and "dead" until the box is opened — a deliberately absurd illustration of the puzzle. How does the fuzzy "both" become a definite "one" the instant we look? That transition is what the interpretations try to explain.

Competing Interpretations

InterpretationWhat it says about measurement
CopenhagenThe wavefunction collapses to one outcome upon measurement
Many-WorldsAll outcomes happen, each in a separate branching universe
Hidden variablesUnknown underlying factors decide the outcome (largely constrained by Bell)

All make the same experimental predictions — they differ only in what they claim is "really" happening.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — superposition before measurement
An electron is in an equal superposition of spin up and spin down. What is the probability of measuring spin up?
1
Equal superposition means equal weight to each outcome.
2
Two equally likely outcomes → each has probability ½.
50% chance of measuring spin up (and 50% spin down).
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 1. What is a "superposition," and what happens to it when you measure the system? Explain below.
Show worked solution

A superposition is a combination of multiple quantum states existing at once. Upon measurement, the system yields a single definite outcome (the wavefunction appears to collapse), with probabilities set by |ψ|².

Multiple states at once; measurement gives one outcome (collapse)
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. How does the Many-Worlds interpretation differ from the Copenhagen interpretation regarding measurement outcomes? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Copenhagen says the wavefunction collapses to one outcome when measured. Many-Worlds says no collapse occurs — instead all outcomes happen, each realized in its own branching universe.

Copenhagen: one outcome (collapse); Many-Worlds: all outcomes, in separate universes
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The interpretations are not different physics — they all predict the same measurable results. They disagree only on the underlying picture of reality. So far, no experiment distinguishes them, which is why the debate remains open.

Key Takeaways
  • Superposition: a system can be in multiple states at once before measurement.
  • Measurement yields one outcome (apparent collapse), with probabilities from |ψ|².
  • Interpretations — Copenhagen, Many-Worlds, hidden variables — explain this differently.
  • They share identical predictions; the difference is philosophical.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Entanglement is the strangest prediction of quantum mechanics — particles linked so that measuring one instantly determines the other, no matter how far apart. Einstein called it "spooky," but it's real, experimentally confirmed, and the powerhouse behind quantum computing and quantum cryptography.

Entangled particles share a single quantum state, so their measurement outcomes are correlated even across vast distances. Bell's theorem proved this cannot be explained by any "hidden" pre-set values — the correlations are deeper than classical intuition allows.

Entanglement

Quantum entanglement
When two particles are entangled, they form one combined state that cannot be described independently. Measuring one instantly determines the corresponding property of the other, regardless of the distance separating them.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
🧠 ANALOGY

It's tempting to picture two gloves split into sealed boxes: open one, find the left glove, and you instantly know the other is right. But entanglement is stranger — Bell's theorem shows the particles do not carry hidden "left/right" labels in advance. The outcome isn't decided until measured, yet the two still match.

Bell's Theorem

Bell's theorem
Bell showed that no theory of "local hidden variables" (pre-determined values carried by each particle) can reproduce quantum predictions. Experiments confirm the quantum correlations, ruling out the comforting classical picture.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — entangled spins
Two electrons are entangled so their spins are always opposite. You measure one and find spin up. What do you instantly know about the other?
1
The entangled state requires opposite spins.
2
If one is measured up, the other must be down.
The other electron is instantly determined to be spin down — even if it's light-years away.
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 1. Two particles are entangled to always give the same result. If one is measured as 0, what will the other give? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Since they are correlated to match, the other will also give 0 — determined instantly upon the first measurement.

0 (the same result)
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. What did Bell's theorem rule out about how entangled particles work? Explain below.
Show worked solution

It ruled out "local hidden variables" — the idea that each particle secretly carries pre-determined values fixed before measurement. The quantum correlations are stronger than any such classical explanation allows.

Local hidden variables (pre-set values) cannot explain the correlations
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Entanglement does not allow faster-than-light communication. Each measurement looks random on its own; the correlation only shows up when the two parties later compare results (via ordinary, slower-than-light channels). No usable signal travels instantly.

Key Takeaways
  • Entangled particles share one state; measuring one instantly determines the other.
  • The correlation holds regardless of distance ("spooky action").
  • Bell's theorem rules out local hidden variables.
  • It does not permit faster-than-light communication.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every particle in the universe is either a fermion or a boson, and this single distinction determines whether particles avoid each other (building up matter) or pile together (enabling lasers and superfluids). It is one of the most fundamental classifications in physics.

All particles fall into two families based on their spin: fermions (half-integer spin) and bosons (integer spin). Fermions are antisocial — they obey Pauli exclusion; bosons are gregarious — they love to share states.

The Two Families

FermionsBosons
SpinHalf-integer (½, 3/2, …)Integer (0, 1, 2, …)
Pauli exclusion?Yes (no sharing)No (can share freely)
ExamplesElectrons, protons, neutronsPhotons, gluons
RoleMake up matterCarry forces
🧠 ANALOGY

Fermions are like introverts at a concert who each insist on their own seat — they build up structure (matter takes up space because electrons refuse to overlap). Bosons are like a crowd happy to pile into the same spot — which is exactly how a laser gets countless photons into one identical state.

Why It Matters Physically

Consequences
Fermions stacking under Pauli exclusion give atoms their shells and make solid matter rigid. Bosons piling into one state make possible lasers (identical photons), superfluids, and Bose-Einstein condensates.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — classify a particle
An electron has spin ½. Is it a fermion or a boson, and does it obey the Pauli exclusion principle?
1
Spin ½ is half-integer → fermion.
2
Fermions obey Pauli exclusion.
The electron is a fermion and obeys the exclusion principle (no two can share a state).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A photon has spin 1. Is it a fermion or a boson? Can many photons occupy the same state? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Spin 1 is an integer → boson. Bosons do not obey Pauli exclusion, so many photons can occupy the same state (this is how lasers work).

Boson; yes, many can share a state
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. A particle has spin 3/2. Which family does it belong to, and does it obey Pauli exclusion? Work below.
Show worked solution

Spin 3/2 is half-integer → fermion. Fermions obey the Pauli exclusion principle.

Fermion; yes, it obeys Pauli exclusion
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The dividing line is half-integer vs integer spin — not "matter vs light." While it's true that matter particles are typically fermions and force carriers bosons, the spin value is the defining criterion. Composite particles can be either, depending on their total spin.

Key Takeaways
  • Fermions (half-integer spin) obey Pauli exclusion; they make up matter.
  • Bosons (integer spin) can share states freely; they carry forces.
  • The criterion is spin: half-integer → fermion, integer → boson.
  • Bosons sharing states enable lasers and Bose-Einstein condensates.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Pauli exclusion principle is why matter has structure at all — why electrons stack into shells instead of all collapsing into the lowest level. It single-handedly explains the periodic table, chemical bonding, and why solid matter takes up space.

The Pauli exclusion principle forbids any two electrons in an atom from occupying the exact same quantum state. This simple rule forces electrons to stack into shells — and that stacking is the periodic table.

The Exclusion Principle

Pauli exclusion principle
No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers (n, ℓ, m_ℓ, m_s). Each orbital (a fixed n, ℓ, m_ℓ) therefore holds at most two electrons — one spin up, one spin down.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
🧠 ANALOGY

Electrons filling an atom are like people filling a stadium where every seat has a unique ticket — no two can share a seat. They fill the cheapest (lowest-energy) seats first and stack upward. The seating chart that results is exactly the electron configuration behind the periodic table.

Building the Periodic Table

Because each orbital holds 2 electrons and each shell has a set number of orbitals, electrons fill up in a fixed order — producing the rows and columns of the periodic table. Elements in the same column have similar outer-electron arrangements, hence similar chemistry.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — electrons in a subshell
The p subshell (ℓ = 1) has 3 orbitals. How many electrons can it hold?
1
Each orbital holds 2 electrons (spin up and spin down).
2
3 orbitals × 2 = 6.
The p subshell holds 6 electrons.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. The s subshell (ℓ = 0) has 1 orbital. How many electrons can it hold? Show your work.
Show worked solution

1 orbital × 2 electrons = 2.

2 electrons
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. The d subshell (ℓ = 2) has 5 orbitals. How many electrons can it hold? Work below.
Show worked solution

5 orbitals × 2 electrons = 10.

10 electrons
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 3. If two electrons are in the same orbital (same n, ℓ, m_ℓ), what must be different about them? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Their spins must differ: one is spin up (m_s = +½), the other spin down (m_s = −½). Otherwise they'd share all four quantum numbers, which Pauli forbids.

Their spins (one +½, one −½)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The exclusion principle applies to fermions (like electrons), not all particles. Bosons (next section) can share a state freely. And it requires all four quantum numbers to match — two electrons can share three of them as long as their spin differs.

Key Takeaways
  • Pauli exclusion: no two electrons share all four quantum numbers.
  • Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons (opposite spins).
  • Subshell capacities: s = 2, p = 6, d = 10 electrons.
  • This stacking builds the periodic table and explains chemistry.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Spin is a purely quantum property with no classical analog — yet it is essential to magnetism, MRI machines, the periodic table, and quantum computing. The Stern-Gerlach experiment revealed it dramatically: a beam of atoms splitting cleanly in two.

Spin is an intrinsic form of angular momentum that quantum particles carry — as if they were tiny magnets, though they are not literally spinning. It is quantized, and the Stern-Gerlach experiment showed this directly.

Intrinsic Angular Momentum

Spin
Spin is a fundamental, built-in angular momentum of a particle, independent of any motion through space. For an electron, the spin quantum number is m_s = +½ or −½ ("spin up" or "spin down") — only two possibilities.
Figure 1. In the Stern-Gerlach experiment, a beam of atoms passing through a non-uniform magnetic field splits into exactly two discrete spots — proof that spin is quantized into just two values.
🧠 ANALOGY

Classically, you'd expect tiny atomic magnets pointing every which way to smear into a continuous band. Instead the beam splits into two sharp spots — as if the magnets are only ever allowed to point fully "up" or fully "down." That all-or-nothing splitting is spin quantization made visible.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — interpreting the split
A beam of silver atoms passes through a Stern-Gerlach magnet and splits into two beams. What does this tell us about electron spin?
1
A classical magnet would give a continuous spread; two discrete spots means the property is quantized.
2
Two spots → exactly two allowed spin values.
Electron spin is quantized into two states: +½ and −½ (up and down).
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 1. How many possible spin states does an electron have, and what are their m_s values? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Two: spin up (m_s = +½) and spin down (m_s = −½).

Two states: m_s = +½ and m_s = −½
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. Why was the result of the Stern-Gerlach experiment surprising from a classical viewpoint? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Classically, atomic magnets oriented randomly should produce a continuous smear of deflections. Instead the beam split into two distinct spots, showing the magnetic property (spin) takes only discrete, quantized values.

Classical physics predicted a continuous smear, not two discrete spots
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Spin is not literal physical rotation — an electron is a point particle and isn't a spinning ball. "Spin" is an intrinsic quantum property that behaves like angular momentum. Taking the spinning-ball picture too literally leads to contradictions.

Key Takeaways
  • Spin is intrinsic angular momentum — a built-in quantum property.
  • An electron has two spin states: m_s = +½ and −½.
  • The Stern-Gerlach experiment split a beam in two, proving spin is quantized.
  • Spin is not literal spinning — it has no classical analog.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The hydrogen atom is the one atom quantum mechanics solves exactly, and its quantum numbers explain the structure of every atom — the shapes of orbitals, the layout of the periodic table, and the rules of chemical bonding. This is where quantum theory meets chemistry.

Solving the Schrödinger equation for hydrogen yields electron states labeled by a set of quantum numbers. These four numbers specify an electron's energy, orbital shape, orientation, and spin — the blueprint of atomic structure.

The Four Quantum Numbers

Quantum numberSymbolDescribes
PrincipalnEnergy level / shell (1, 2, 3, …)
Angular momentumℓOrbital shape (0 to n−1; s, p, d, f)
Magneticm_ℓOrbital orientation (−ℓ to +ℓ)
Spinm_sElectron spin (+½ or −½)
Hydrogen energy levels
As in the Bohr model, the energy depends only on n: E_n = −13.6/n² eV. But the full quantum treatment adds the orbital shapes and orientations that Bohr's simple circles could not capture.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
🧠 ANALOGY

The quantum numbers are like an address for each electron: n is the floor of the building, ℓ is the wing, m_ℓ is the specific room, and m_s is which of two beds. No two electrons in an atom can share the exact same full address — the rule that builds the periodic table.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — allowed values of ℓ
For an electron with principal quantum number n = 3, what values can the angular momentum quantum number ℓ take?
1
The rule is ℓ = 0, 1, 2, …, up to n − 1.
2
With n = 3, ℓ can be 0, 1, or 2.
ℓ = 0, 1, 2 (the 3s, 3p, and 3d subshells).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. For n = 2, what values can ℓ take? (ℓ ranges from 0 to n − 1.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

ℓ goes from 0 to n − 1 = 1. So ℓ = 0 or 1 (the 2s and 2p subshells).

ℓ = 0, 1
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. For ℓ = 1, what values can the magnetic quantum number m_ℓ take, and how many orbitals is that? (m_ℓ ranges from −ℓ to +ℓ.) Work below.
Show worked solution

m_ℓ ranges from −1 to +1: that is −1, 0, +1 — three values, so three orbitals (the three p orbitals).

m_ℓ = −1, 0, +1 (3 orbitals)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The quantum numbers are nested: ℓ depends on n (max n−1), and m_ℓ depends on ℓ (from −ℓ to +ℓ). You cannot pick them independently — for example, ℓ = 2 is impossible when n = 2. Always respect the hierarchy.

Key Takeaways
  • Four quantum numbers label each electron state: n, ℓ, m_ℓ, m_s.
  • n = energy/shell, ℓ = shape, m_ℓ = orientation, m_s = spin.
  • They are nested: ℓ ≤ n−1, and −ℓ ≤ m_ℓ ≤ +ℓ.
  • Hydrogen energy: E_n = −13.6/n² eV; the numbers underlie the periodic table.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The quantum harmonic oscillator models any system near a stable equilibrium — vibrating molecules, atoms in crystals, even quantum fields. Its evenly spaced energy levels and nonzero ground-state energy are among the most reused results in all of physics.

The quantum version of a mass on a spring has evenly spaced energy levels — unlike the box, where they spread apart. It also has a nonzero lowest energy, and it describes molecular vibrations and much more.

Equally Spaced Levels

Harmonic oscillator energies
E_n = (n + ½)ℏω, with n = 0, 1, 2, …, where ω is the classical angular frequency. The levels are equally spaced by ℏω, and the lowest (n = 0) energy is ½ℏω — the zero-point energy.
Figure 1. Inside the parabolic potential, the energy levels are evenly spaced by ℏω — a signature of the harmonic oscillator (contrast the box, whose gaps widen).
🧠 ANALOGY

The oscillator's levels are like a perfectly even ladder — each rung the same distance apart (ℏω). And the bottom rung sits above the floor (½ℏω): even in its lowest state, the system still "jiggles." That residual motion is the zero-point energy.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — level spacing
A quantum oscillator has level spacing ℏω = 0.5 eV. Find the energy of the ground state (n = 0) and the first excited state (n = 1).
1
Ground state: E₀ = (0 + ½)ℏω = ½(0.5) = 0.25 eV.
2
First excited: E₁ = (1 + ½)ℏω = 1.5(0.5) = 0.75 eV.
E₀ = 0.25 eV, E₁ = 0.75 eV (a gap of 0.5 eV = ℏω).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A quantum oscillator has ℏω = 2 eV. Find the ground-state energy (n = 0). (E_n = (n + ½)ℏω.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

E₀ = (0 + ½)(2) = 0.5 × 2 = 1 eV.

E₀ = 1 eV
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. For an oscillator with ℏω = 2 eV, find the energies of n = 1 and n = 2, and confirm the spacing. Work below.
Show worked solution

E₁ = (1.5)(2) = 3 eV. E₂ = (2.5)(2) = 5 eV. Spacing = 5 − 3 = 2 eV = ℏω. ✓ Equally spaced.

E₁ = 3 eV, E₂ = 5 eV; spacing = 2 eV
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Here the quantum number starts at n = 0 (unlike the box's n = 1). The ground state is n = 0 with energy ½ℏω — still nonzero. And the levels are equally spaced, not n²-spaced like the box; don't mix the two models.

Key Takeaways
  • Harmonic oscillator: E_n = (n + ½)ℏω, n = 0, 1, 2, …
  • Levels are equally spaced by ℏω.
  • Ground-state (zero-point) energy is ½ℏω — nonzero.
  • Models molecular vibrations and systems near equilibrium.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Quantum tunneling lets particles pass through barriers they classically could never cross — a purely quantum phenomenon with huge consequences. It powers the Sun's fusion, radioactive decay, scanning tunneling microscopes, and the flash memory in your devices.

Tunneling is the ability of a quantum particle to pass through an energy barrier even when it lacks the energy to go "over" it classically. The wavefunction leaks through, giving a real probability of appearing on the far side.

Passing Through the Impossible

Quantum tunneling
When a particle meets a barrier taller than its energy, its wavefunction does not stop dead — it decays exponentially inside the barrier and emerges with reduced amplitude on the other side. There is a nonzero probability the particle is found beyond the barrier.
Figure 1. The wavefunction decays inside the barrier (dashed) but emerges with smaller amplitude on the far side — a nonzero chance the particle tunnels through.
🧠 ANALOGY

Classically, a ball rolled at a hill it can't climb always rolls back. Quantum mechanically, it's as if the ball occasionally just appears on the other side — having "tunneled" through. The thinner or lower the hill, the more often it happens.

Real-World Tunneling

Tunneling is not exotic — it is everywhere: nuclear fusion in the Sun (protons tunnel to fuse), alpha decay (particles tunnel out of nuclei), the scanning tunneling microscope (imaging individual atoms), and flash memory (electrons tunnel to store data).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — what affects tunneling
Two barriers are identical in height, but barrier A is thicker than barrier B. Through which is a particle more likely to tunnel?
1
Tunneling probability decreases exponentially with barrier thickness.
2
The thinner barrier (B) allows much more tunneling.
The particle tunnels far more easily through the thinner barrier B.
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 1. A particle has less energy than a barrier is tall. Classically, can it cross? Quantum mechanically, can it? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Classically, no — it lacks the energy and always reflects. Quantum mechanically, yes: its wavefunction leaks through, so there is a nonzero probability of finding it on the other side (tunneling).

Classically no; quantum mechanically yes (tunneling)
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. Name one real-world device or process that relies on quantum tunneling. Work below.
Show worked solution

Any of: nuclear fusion in stars, alpha (radioactive) decay, the scanning tunneling microscope, flash/USB memory, or tunnel diodes.

e.g. scanning tunneling microscope, flash memory, alpha decay, stellar fusion
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Tunneling does not mean the particle gains energy to leap the barrier — its energy is unchanged. The wavefunction simply has a small amplitude beyond the barrier. And tunneling probability drops exponentially with barrier width and height, so thick barriers make it astronomically rare.

Key Takeaways
  • Tunneling: a particle can pass through a barrier it classically cannot cross.
  • The wavefunction decays exponentially inside the barrier but emerges beyond it.
  • Probability drops sharply with barrier thickness and height.
  • Powers fusion, radioactive decay, STM imaging, and flash memory.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The particle in a box is the "hydrogen atom of quantum learning" — the simplest solvable system, yet it reveals the deepest quantum truths: confinement forces energy to be quantized, and a particle can never be perfectly at rest. It models quantum dots, molecules, and more.

Trap a particle between two walls and quantum mechanics produces something remarkable: only specific energy levels are allowed, exactly like the standing waves on a string. This simple model shows where quantization comes from.

Quantized Energies

Particle in a box
For a particle of mass m confined to a 1-D box of length L, the allowed energies are E_n = n²h² / (8mL²), with n = 1, 2, 3, …. The wavefunctions are standing waves that must vanish at both walls.
Figure 1. Energy levels in a box grow as n² (1, 4, 9, 16…), so the gaps widen at higher n. The walls confine the particle and force quantization.
🧠 ANALOGY

A trapped quantum particle is like a jump rope fixed at both ends: only whole-number patterns of waves fit (one hump, two humps, three…). Each pattern is an allowed state with its own energy. You can never have "half a hump" — that's quantization, and it's why the lowest energy isn't zero.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — energy levels scale as n²
If the ground state (n = 1) of a particle in a box has energy 2 eV, what is the energy of the n = 3 level?
1
E_n = n²·E₁ (energies scale as n²).
2
E₃ = 3² × 2 = 9 × 2.
E₃ = 18 eV.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. The ground state of a particle in a box is 1.5 eV. Find the energy of the n = 2 level. (E_n = n²E₁.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

E₂ = 2² × 1.5 = 4 × 1.5 = 6 eV.

E₂ = 6 eV
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. Can a particle in a box have zero energy (be perfectly at rest)? Explain why or why not. Work below.
Show worked solution

No. The lowest level is n = 1 (n = 0 would mean ψ = 0 everywhere — no particle). So the minimum energy E₁ is nonzero. This is the "zero-point energy" — a confined quantum particle is never perfectly still (consistent with the uncertainty principle).

No — the ground state (n=1) has nonzero energy (zero-point energy)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The quantum number starts at n = 1, not n = 0 (n = 0 gives a zero wavefunction — no particle). So the lowest energy is positive: a trapped particle always retains some minimum "zero-point" energy and can never be completely at rest.

Key Takeaways
  • Particle in a box: E_n = n²h²/(8mL²), with n = 1, 2, 3, …
  • Energies scale as n² (gaps widen at higher levels).

Quantum mechanics represents every measurable quantity — energy, position, momentum — by a mathematical operator. This framework is what makes quantum predictions precise and is the language of all advanced quantum theory, from chemistry to quantum computing.

In quantum mechanics, measurable quantities (observables) are represented by operators that act on the wavefunction. The possible measurement results are the operator's eigenvalues, and averages are given by expectation values.

Observables as Operators

Operators and eigenvalues
Each observable (energy, momentum, position…) has an operator. When the operator acts on a wavefunction and returns a multiple of it (operator·ψ = a·ψ), the value a is a possible measurement outcome (an eigenvalue), and ψ is an eigenstate.
Expectation value
The expectation value ⟨A⟩ is the average result you would get from many measurements on identically prepared systems. It need not be any single allowed value — it is the statistical mean.
🧠 ANALOGY

Think of an operator as a "question" you pose to the wavefunction, and the eigenvalues as the only valid "answers" nature will give. The expectation value is the average answer over many trials — like the mean of many dice rolls (3.5), even though no single roll gives 3.5.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — eigenvalue as outcome
An energy operator acting on a state gives Ĥψ = 4ψ (in eV). What energy will a measurement yield?
1
The operator returns a multiple of ψ, so ψ is an energy eigenstate.
2
The eigenvalue (the multiplier) is the measured energy.
A measurement gives exactly 4 eV.
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 1. An operator acts on a wavefunction and returns 7 times that same wavefunction. What does the number 7 represent? Explain below.
Show worked solution

The 7 is an eigenvalue — a possible result of measuring that observable. The wavefunction is an eigenstate, so the measurement yields 7 with certainty.

7 is an eigenvalue — a possible (here certain) measurement result
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. What is the difference between an eigenvalue and an expectation value? Explain below.
Show worked solution

An eigenvalue is one specific possible outcome of a single measurement. An expectation value is the average outcome over many measurements on identically prepared systems — it may not equal any single allowed eigenvalue.

Eigenvalue = a possible single result; expectation value = the average over many measurements
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The expectation value is an average, not a prediction for any one measurement — and it can be a value the system can never actually return in a single measurement (just as the average die roll, 3.5, never appears on a die). Don't confuse it with an allowed outcome.

Key Takeaways
  • Observables are represented by operators acting on the wavefunction.
  • An operator's eigenvalues are the possible measurement outcomes.
  • The expectation value ⟨A⟩ is the average over many measurements.
  • An average need not be an allowed single result.
📊 FIGURE — compatible and incompatible observables
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Testing compatibility by multiplying in both orders

Two observables can be known exactly at the same time only if their operators commute — only if applying them in either order gives the same result. The test is the commutator [A, B] = AB − BA: zero means compatible, non-zero means an uncertainty relation binds them.

Spin along x and along z, as Pauli matrices:

import numpy as np
sx = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]], dtype=complex)
sz = np.array([[1,0],[0,-1]], dtype=complex)
print(sx@sz - sz@sx)
[[ 0.+0.j -2.+0.j] [ 2.+0.j 0.+0.j]]
computed with NumPy 2.4.6

Not zero — it comes out to exactly −2iσy (checked: True). So spin-x and spin-z are incompatible: measure one sharply and the other is left completely undetermined. Position and momentum are the famous case, [x, p] = iℏ, and the ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2 relation is its direct consequence.

By contrast [σz, σz] = 0 — anything commutes with itself, which is just to say a measurement repeated immediately gives the same answer.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming any two quantities can be pinned down together with enough care. Whether they can is fixed by the algebra, not by effort: if the commutator is non-zero, no experiment, however perfect, can make both sharp at once.
🎯 EXAM TIP
"Commute" is the exam word. A question phrased as "can both be known simultaneously / exactly / precisely" is asking one thing: do their operators commute? Commuting operators also share eigenstates — a single state can be sharp in both.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The uncertainty principle is one of the most famous and misunderstood ideas in science. It sets a hard limit on what can be known — not from clumsy instruments, but as a fundamental feature of reality. It shapes everything from atomic stability to quantum technology.

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says you cannot simultaneously know a particle's exact position and exact momentum. The more precisely you pin down one, the more uncertain the other becomes — built into nature itself.

The Principle

Uncertainty principle
Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2, where Δx is the uncertainty in position, Δp the uncertainty in momentum, and ℏ = h/2π ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. Shrinking one uncertainty forces the other to grow.
🧠 ANALOGY

It is like a blurry photo of a speeding car. Use a fast shutter and you freeze its position sharply — but lose all sense of how fast it's moving. Use a long exposure to capture its motion (a streak) and its position smears out. You fundamentally cannot have both perfectly sharp at once.

It Is Not About Measurement Clumsiness

This is not a technological limitation — even with perfect instruments, the limit holds. A particle simply does not possess both a precise position and a precise momentum at the same time. It is a statement about reality, not about our tools.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — minimum momentum uncertainty
An electron's position is known to within Δx = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Find the minimum uncertainty in its momentum. (ℏ = 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
1
At the limit, Δx · Δp = ℏ/2, so Δp = ℏ/(2·Δx).
2
Δp = (1.05 × 10⁻³⁴)/(2 × 1 × 10⁻¹⁰) = (1.05 × 10⁻³⁴)/(2 × 10⁻¹⁰).
Δp ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s — the smallest possible momentum uncertainty for that position precision.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A particle's position is known to within Δx = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Find the minimum momentum uncertainty. (Δp = ℏ/(2Δx), ℏ = 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

Δp = ℏ/(2Δx) = (1.05 × 10⁻³⁴)/(2 × 2 × 10⁻¹⁰) = (1.05 × 10⁻³⁴)/(4 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s.

Δp ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. If you measure a particle's position more and more precisely (smaller Δx), what happens to the uncertainty in its momentum? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Since Δx·Δp ≥ ℏ/2, making Δx smaller forces Δp to grow larger. Perfect position knowledge (Δx → 0) would make momentum completely uncertain.

The momentum uncertainty Δp grows larger
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The uncertainty principle is not about the measurement disturbing the particle or imperfect equipment. It is a fundamental property: a particle genuinely does not have both a definite position and definite momentum simultaneously, regardless of how it is measured.

Key Takeaways
  • Uncertainty principle: Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2.
  • You cannot simultaneously know exact position and exact momentum.
  • It is a fundamental limit of nature, not a measurement flaw.
  • ℏ = h/2π ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
📊 FIGURE — where uncertainty comes from
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why a particle cannot have both at once

The uncertainty principle is not a statement about clumsy equipment. It follows from the fact that a particle is a wave, and it would hold for a perfect instrument.

De Broglie ties momentum to wavelength (p = h/λ), so a definite momentum means a single wavelength — and a pure single-wavelength wave stretches endlessly through space, giving no position at all. To build a localised bump you must add many wavelengths together; the tighter the bump, the wider the range of wavelengths, and therefore the wider the range of momenta. Sharpening Δx necessarily widens Δp. That trade is a property of waves, not of laboratories.

Pinning an electron to an atom-sized 0.1 nm:

dx = 1e-10 m dp >= hbar/(2 dx) = 5.27286e-25 kg m/s dv >= 578838 m/s
computed with NumPy 2.4.6

Confining it that tightly forces a velocity spread of roughly 5.8 × 10⁵ m/s — nearly 0.2% of the speed of light. That is why electrons cannot simply sit still inside an atom.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
The "you disturb it by looking" story. It is the standard explanation and it is wrong — or at best a loose analogy. Uncertainty is built into what a quantum state is: the particle does not secretly possess an exact position and momentum that measurement spoils. It has no such pair of values to begin with.
🎯 EXAM TIP
The same trade-off appears in ordinary signal processing: a very short sound pulse has no definite pitch, and a pure tone has no definite moment. Position–momentum is that identical wave relationship, with Planck’s constant setting the scale.

The Schrödinger equation is to quantum mechanics what Newton's second law is to classical mechanics — the master equation governing everything. Solving it yields the allowed energies and wavefunctions of atoms, molecules, and materials. It is the engine of the quantum world.

The Schrödinger equation determines how quantum systems behave. Solving it gives the allowed wavefunctions and their energies — and crucially, only certain discrete energies are permitted for bound systems.

The Master Equation

Time-independent Schrödinger equation
In compact form, Ĥψ = Eψ, where Ĥ is the Hamiltonian (the total-energy operator), ψ is the wavefunction, and E is the energy. Solving it finds the allowed (ψ, E) pairs for a system.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
Quantization from boundary conditions
For a bound particle, only wavefunctions that "fit" the boundaries are valid — this is what forces energy to be quantized into discrete levels, rather than continuous.
🧠 ANALOGY

Think of a guitar string fixed at both ends: only certain wavelengths "fit" and produce standing waves (the harmonics). The Schrödinger equation plays the same role for a trapped particle — only certain wavefunctions fit the boundaries, and each corresponds to one allowed energy. That is where quantized energy levels come from.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — interpreting Ĥψ = Eψ
A wavefunction ψ satisfies Ĥψ = Eψ with E = 5 eV. What does this mean physically?
1
ψ is an allowed quantum state of the system (an "energy eigenstate").
2
The constant E is the definite energy of that state.
A particle in state ψ has a definite energy of 5 eV — one of the system's allowed levels.
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 1. In the equation Ĥψ = Eψ, what does Ĥ represent and what does E tell you? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Ĥ is the Hamiltonian, the total-energy operator for the system. E is the energy of the state ψ — a specific allowed energy value (an eigenvalue).

Ĥ = total-energy operator; E = the state's (allowed) energy
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. Why are the energies of a bound quantum system (like an electron in an atom) discrete rather than continuous? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Only wavefunctions that satisfy the boundary conditions (that "fit" the confining region) are valid solutions of the Schrödinger equation. Just like standing waves on a string, only specific patterns fit — and each corresponds to one discrete allowed energy.

Only wavefunctions fitting the boundaries are allowed → discrete energies
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The Schrödinger equation does not give a particle's trajectory (there is no definite path in quantum mechanics). It gives the wavefunction, from which only probabilities follow. Quantization of energy is a result of solving it under boundary conditions, not a separate assumption.

Key Takeaways
  • The Schrödinger equation (Ĥψ = Eψ) is the master equation of quantum mechanics.
  • Solving it yields the allowed wavefunctions and energies.
  • Boundary conditions force energy to be quantized (like standing waves).
  • It predicts probabilities, not trajectories.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The wavefunction is the central object of quantum mechanics — it contains everything knowable about a system. But it describes only probabilities, a radical break from classical certainty. Understanding it is understanding how nature works at the deepest level.

In quantum mechanics, a particle is described not by a definite position but by a wavefunction ψ spread over space. Its square gives the probability of finding the particle — quantum mechanics is fundamentally probabilistic.

The Wavefunction and the Born Rule

Wavefunction
The wavefunction ψ(x) encodes the complete quantum state of a particle. It is generally spread out, not located at a single point.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
Born rule (probability)
|ψ(x)|² is the probability density — the probability of finding the particle near position x. Where |ψ|² is large, the particle is likely; where it is zero, the particle is never found.
Normalization
Since the particle must be somewhere, the total probability over all space equals 1: the area under |ψ|² is 1. A valid wavefunction must be normalized.
🧠 ANALOGY

The wavefunction is like a smeared cloud of "likelihood." Before you measure, the particle isn't at one spot — it's a cloud denser in some regions than others. |ψ|² is the cloud's density. Measure it, and the cloud abruptly collapses to the single point where you found it.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — reading probability density
A particle's |ψ|² is twice as large at point A as at point B. Where is the particle more likely to be found, and by how much?
1
Probability is proportional to |ψ|².
2
|ψ|² at A is 2× that at B, so the particle is twice as likely at A.
The particle is twice as likely to be found at A as at B.
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 1. At a certain point, the wavefunction ψ = 0. What is the probability of finding the particle exactly there? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Probability density is |ψ|². If ψ = 0, then |ψ|² = 0, so the particle is never found at that point (such points are called nodes).

Zero — the particle is never found where ψ = 0
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. Why must a wavefunction be "normalized," and what does the total area under |ψ|² equal? Explain below.
Show worked solution

The particle must exist somewhere, so the probability of finding it anywhere in all space must total 100%. Thus the total area under |ψ|² equals 1.

So total probability = 1 (the area under |ψ|² is 1)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

It is |ψ|², not ψ itself, that gives probability. The wavefunction can be negative or even complex; squaring its magnitude makes a proper (non-negative) probability. Never interpret ψ directly as a probability.

Key Takeaways
  • The wavefunction ψ contains all information about a quantum state.
  • |ψ|² is the probability density (the Born rule).
  • A valid wavefunction is normalized: total probability = 1.
  • Quantum mechanics predicts probabilities, not definite outcomes.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Wave-particle duality is the central mystery of quantum mechanics: everything — light and matter — behaves as both wave and particle. De Broglie's insight that electrons have wavelengths underlies electron microscopes and the entire quantum description of atoms.

Light acts as a wave (interference) and a particle (photons). de Broglie made the stunning leap: matter does too. Every particle has a wavelength, and this duality is the foundation of quantum mechanics.

Duality and Matter Waves

Wave-particle duality
Light and matter both exhibit wave behavior (interference, diffraction) and particle behavior (localized impacts). Which shows up depends on the experiment — but both are always present.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
de Broglie wavelength
Any particle with momentum p has a wavelength λ = h/p, where h is Planck's constant. Heavier or faster particles have shorter wavelengths — which is why everyday objects show no visible wave behavior.
🧠 ANALOGY

In the double-slit experiment, even single electrons fired one at a time slowly build up an interference pattern — as if each electron passed through both slits as a wave, then landed as a particle. Matter genuinely has a wave nature; we just never notice it for big objects because their wavelengths are absurdly tiny.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — de Broglie wavelength
Find the de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum 2 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
1
λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)/(2 × 10⁻²⁴).
2
= 3.315 × 10⁻³⁴⁺²⁴ = 3.315 × 10⁻¹⁰.
λ ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (about the size of an atom).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find the de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum 3 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s. (λ = h/p, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)/(3 × 10⁻²⁴) = 2.21 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

λ ≈ 2.21 × 10⁻¹⁰ m
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. Why don't we notice the wave nature of everyday objects like a baseball? Explain below.
Show worked solution

A baseball's momentum is enormous compared to h, so its de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p is unimaginably tiny (far smaller than an atom). Wave effects like interference are undetectable at that scale.

Its momentum is huge, so λ = h/p is far too small to detect
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Duality does not mean a particle is "sometimes a wave and sometimes a particle" as if switching. It is always both; the experiment determines which aspect is revealed. And matter waves are very real — electron diffraction is measured routinely — just invisible for macroscopic objects.

Key Takeaways
  • Wave-particle duality: light and matter are both wave-like and particle-like.
  • de Broglie wavelength: λ = h/p for any particle.
  • Big objects have negligibly small wavelengths — hence no visible wave behavior.
  • The double-slit experiment reveals matter's wave nature directly.

The Bohr model explained why atoms emit only specific colors of light — the barcode-like spectra that identify every element. It introduced quantized energy levels, the idea at the heart of all of atomic physics, chemistry, lasers, and neon signs.

Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus only in specific energy levels. Jumping between levels emits or absorbs a photon of an exact energy — explaining the sharp, discrete lines in atomic spectra.

Quantized Energy Levels

Bohr model
Electrons occupy only discrete energy levels labeled by n = 1, 2, 3, …. For hydrogen, E_n = −13.6/n² eV. The lowest level (n = 1) is the most negative (most tightly bound) ground state.
Photon emission/absorption
An electron jumps levels by emitting (dropping) or absorbing (rising) a photon whose energy equals the gap: E_photon = |E_final − E_initial|. Only these exact energies appear — hence discrete spectral lines.
Figure 1. Discrete energy levels. Dropping to a lower level emits a photon (red); absorbing a photon kicks the electron up (green). The photon energy exactly equals the gap.
🧠 ANALOGY

Energy levels are like rungs on a ladder — an electron can stand on a rung but never between them. To move up, it must absorb exactly enough energy to reach a rung; dropping down releases exactly that rung-gap as a photon. The fixed gaps make fixed colors.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — energy of a transition
In hydrogen, find the energy of the photon emitted when an electron drops from n = 2 to n = 1. (E_n = −13.6/n² eV)
1
E₂ = −13.6/2² = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV. E₁ = −13.6/1² = −13.6 eV.
2
Photon energy = |E₁ − E₂| = |−13.6 − (−3.4)| = |−10.2|.
E_photon = 10.2 eV (an ultraviolet photon).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find the energy of the n = 3 level of hydrogen. (E_n = −13.6/n².) Show your work.
Show worked solution

E₃ = −13.6/3² = −13.6/9 ≈ −1.51 eV.

E₃ ≈ −1.51 eV
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. Find the energy of the photon emitted when a hydrogen electron drops from n = 3 to n = 2. (Use E₃ ≈ −1.51 eV and E₂ = −3.4 eV.) Work below.
Show worked solution

Photon energy = |E₂ − E₃| = |−3.4 − (−1.51)| = |−1.89| = 1.89 eV (a red visible photon — the famous H-alpha line).

E_photon ≈ 1.89 eV
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Energy levels are negative (bound states), and n = 1 is the lowest (most negative) energy, not the highest. As n increases, energy rises toward 0 (the electron becomes less bound). Be careful with the signs when computing gaps.

Key Takeaways
  • The Bohr model: electrons occupy discrete energy levels (E_n = −13.6/n² eV for hydrogen).
  • Jumps emit/absorb a photon with energy equal to the level gap.
  • This explains discrete atomic spectra — each element's fingerprint.
  • Levels are negative; n = 1 is the ground state (most bound).

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The photoelectric effect proved light itself is quantized into photons — and won Einstein his Nobel Prize. It is direct evidence that light is not purely a wave, and it powers solar panels, digital cameras, and light sensors everywhere.

Shine light on a metal and it can eject electrons — but the details defied wave theory. Einstein explained it by treating light as a stream of photons, each a packet of energy E = hf.

What Puzzled Classical Physics

Wave theory said brighter light (more energy) should eject electrons more energetically. Instead, experiments showed the electrons' energy depends on the light's frequency, not its brightness — and below a threshold frequency, no electrons come out no matter how bright the light.

Einstein's Photon Explanation

Photon
Light is made of photons, particles each carrying energy E = hf. One photon ejects one electron. A brighter beam has more photons, but each still carries the same energy hf.
Photoelectric equation
KE_max = hf − φ: the ejected electron's maximum kinetic energy equals the photon energy minus the work function φ (the energy needed to free an electron from the metal). Below φ, nothing escapes.
🧠 ANALOGY

Think of electrons trapped in a pit. A photon is a single ball thrown in; only a ball with enough energy (high enough frequency) can knock an electron out. Throwing many weak balls (bright, low-frequency light) does nothing — no single one clears the wall. Energy comes one photon at a time.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — photoelectric effect
A photon of energy 5 eV strikes a metal with work function 2 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electron.
1
KE_max = hf − φ = (photon energy) − (work function) = 5 − 2.
KE_max = 3 eV.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A photon of energy 7 eV hits a metal with work function 3 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electron. Show your work.
Show worked solution

KE_max = hf − φ = 7 − 3 = 4 eV.

KE_max = 4 eV
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. A metal has work function 4 eV. A photon of energy 3 eV strikes it. Will an electron be ejected? Why or why not? Explain below.
Show worked solution

No. The photon energy (3 eV) is less than the work function (4 eV), so it cannot free an electron — regardless of how bright the light is. KE_max would be negative, which is impossible.

No — photon energy (3 eV) is below the work function (4 eV)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Brightness (intensity) sets the number of electrons ejected, but only frequency sets each electron's energy. A very bright low-frequency light ejects nothing; a dim high-frequency light ejects energetic electrons. This frequency-not-brightness dependence is the whole point.

Key Takeaways
  • The photoelectric effect shows light is quantized into photons (E = hf).
  • KE_max = hf − φ, where φ is the work function.
  • Electron energy depends on frequency, not brightness; below a threshold, none escape.
  • Brightness sets the number of photons/electrons, not their energy.
📊 FIGURE — stopping potential
s = KEmaxin eV and voltsthe numbers are equaldepends onfrequency and the work functiondoes NOT depend onintensity / brightnessbrighter lightmore electrons, same Vs
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Measuring KEmax with a voltage

You cannot weigh a photoelectron’s energy directly, so the experiment applies a reverse voltage that pushes the electrons back. Turn it up until even the fastest electron just fails to reach the collector and the current drops to zero. That voltage is the stopping potential Vs.

An electron crossing V volts changes energy by exactly V electron-volts, so eVs = KEmax — and in these units the numbers match: KEmax = 1.5 eV gives Vs = 1.5 V.

Working it from the light instead, using hc = 1239.84 eV·nm:

lambda = 400 nm -> E = 3.0996 eV work function phi = 2.0 eV KE_max = 3.0996 - 2.0 = 1.0996 eV -> V_s = 1.0996 V
computed with NumPy 2.4.6

So 400 nm light on a metal of work function 2.0 eV needs about 1.10 V to stop the photocurrent.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Expecting a brighter lamp to need a bigger stopping potential. It does not. Brightness adds more photons, so more electrons flow — a larger current — but each photon still carries hf, so KEmax and therefore Vs are unchanged. Only changing the frequency moves the stopping potential.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Memorise hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm. Then a photon’s energy in eV is just 1240 divided by its wavelength in nm — no Planck constant, no joules, no unit conversion.

This is where quantum physics was born. In 1900, classical physics made an absurd prediction about glowing objects — infinite energy — and Planck's radical fix, that energy comes in discrete chunks, cracked the universe open. Every quantum idea descends from this moment.

A hot object glows — and explaining the color of that glow shattered classical physics. The classical prediction blew up to infinity (the "ultraviolet catastrophe"), and Planck fixed it only by assuming energy is quantized.

The Ultraviolet Catastrophe

Blackbody radiation
A blackbody is an ideal object that absorbs and re-emits all radiation; the spectrum of its glow depends only on temperature. Classical physics predicted the intensity would rise without limit at short wavelengths — infinite total energy, the absurd ultraviolet catastrophe.

Planck's Quantum Hypothesis

Planck's hypothesis
Planck proposed that energy is emitted only in discrete packets ("quanta") of size E = hf, where f is frequency and h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant. This single assumption removed the catastrophe and matched experiment perfectly.
Figure 1. Classical theory (dashed) shoots to infinity at short wavelengths — the ultraviolet catastrophe. Planck's quantized energy (solid) gives the correct, finite, peaked curve.
🧠 ANALOGY

Classical energy was like a ramp — any amount allowed, smoothly. Planck said it is really a staircase: you can only have energy in whole-step amounts (hf each). At high frequencies the steps are huge, so they are rarely "climbed" — which tames the runaway and kills the catastrophe.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — energy of a quantum
Find the energy of one quantum of light with frequency 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
1
E = hf = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)(5 × 10¹⁴).
2
= 6.63 × 5 × 10⁻³⁴⁺¹⁴ = 33.15 × 10⁻²⁰.
E ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J — a tiny but discrete packet of energy.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find the energy of a quantum of light with frequency 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (E = hf, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

E = hf = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)(6 × 10¹⁴) = 39.78 × 10⁻²⁰ ≈ 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

E ≈ 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. In one sentence, what was the "ultraviolet catastrophe," and what assumption did Planck make to resolve it? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Classical physics predicted a blackbody would radiate infinite energy at short (ultraviolet) wavelengths; Planck resolved it by assuming energy is quantized in packets of E = hf.

Classical theory predicted infinite UV energy; Planck quantized energy (E = hf)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Quantization means energy comes in discrete multiples of hf — not any value. Because h is so tiny, these steps are imperceptible for everyday objects, which is why classical physics seemed to work. Quantization only becomes obvious at atomic scales.

Key Takeaways
  • Classical physics predicted the ultraviolet catastrophe — infinite blackbody energy.
  • Planck resolved it by quantizing energy: E = hf.
  • h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s (Planck's constant) — the new fundamental constant.
  • This was the birth of quantum physics.
📊 FIGURE — Wien’s displacement law
max T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·Khotter objectpeak moves to SHORTER wavelengthcooler objectpeak moves to longer wavelengthdouble the temperaturehalve the peak wavelengthtells youWHERE the spectrum peaksStefan–BoltzmannHOW MUCH total energy (∝ T⁴)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Reading a temperature off a colour

Wien’s displacement law pins where a blackbody’s glow is brightest: λmax = b / T, with b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K.

T = 5800 K -> lambda_max = 4.99655e-07 m = 499.7 nm T = 3000 K -> lambda_max = 9.66e-07 m = 966 nm T = 300 K -> lambda_max = 9.66e-06 m = 9660 nm
computed with NumPy 2.4.6
  • The Sun at ~5800 K peaks at about 500 nm — green-yellow, right in the middle of the visible band our eyes evolved to use.
  • A 3000 K filament peaks at 966 nm, in the infrared: most of its output is heat, not light, which is why incandescent bulbs are so wasteful.
  • You, at roughly 300 K, peak near 9660 nm — deep infrared. That is what a thermal camera sees.

The relationship is inverse, so doubling the temperature halves the peak wavelength: the ratio λ(5800) / λ(11600) computes to exactly 2.0. Hotter always means shorter — that is why a heating element glows dull red first, then orange, then white as it gets hotter.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Mixing up the two blackbody laws. Wien tells you where the peak sits (λmax ∝ 1/T); Stefan–Boltzmann tells you how much total power comes out (∝ T⁴). A question about colour is Wien; a question about total energy is Stefan–Boltzmann.
🎯 EXAM TIP
If a question says "hotter", answer shorter wavelength / higher frequency / bluer. The word "displacement" in the name is the hint: raising T displaces the peak toward the blue end.

📋 The Quantum Revolution

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Blackbody Radiation & the UV Catastrophe

▸ Blackbody radiation A blackbody is an ideal object that absorbs and re-emits all radiation; the spectrum of its glow depends only on temperature. Classical physics predicted the intensity would rise without limit at short wavelengths — infinite total energy, the absurd ultraviolet catastrophe .

▸ Planck's hypothesis Planck proposed that energy is emitted only in discrete packets ("quanta") of size E = hf , where f is frequency and h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant. This single assumption removed the catastrophe and matched experiment perfectly.

The Photoelectric Effect & Photons

▸ Photon Light is made of photons , particles each carrying energy E = hf . One photon ejects one electron. A brighter beam has more photons, but each still carries the same energy hf.

▸ Photoelectric equation KE_max = hf − φ : the ejected electron's maximum kinetic energy equals the photon energy minus the work function φ (the energy needed to free an electron from the metal). Below φ, nothing escapes.

The Bohr Model & Atomic Spectra

▸ Bohr model Electrons occupy only discrete energy levels labeled by n = 1, 2, 3, …. For hydrogen, E_n = −13.6/n² eV . The lowest level (n = 1) is the most negative (most tightly bound) ground state.

▸ Photon emission/absorption An electron jumps levels by emitting (dropping) or absorbing (rising) a photon whose energy equals the gap: E_photon = |E_final − E_initial| . Only these exact energies appear — hence discrete spectral lines.

Wave-Particle Duality & de Broglie

▸ Wave-particle duality Light and matter both exhibit wave behavior (interference, diffraction) and particle behavior (localized impacts). Which shows up depends on the experiment — but both are always present.

▸ de Broglie wavelength Any particle with momentum p has a wavelength λ = h/p , where h is Planck's constant. Heavier or faster particles have shorter wavelengths — which is why everyday objects show no visible wave behavior.

"},"PHYSQ/cheat/c2":{"body":"

📋 Wave Mechanics

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

The Wavefunction & Probability

▸ Wavefunction The wavefunction ψ(x) encodes the complete quantum state of a particle. It is generally spread out, not located at a single point.

▸ Born rule (probability) |ψ(x)|² is the probability density — the probability of finding the particle near position x. Where |ψ|² is large, the particle is likely; where it is zero, the particle is never found.

▸ Normalization Since the particle must be somewhere , the total probability over all space equals 1: the area under |ψ|² is 1. A valid wavefunction must be normalized .

The Schrodinger Equation

▸ Time-independent Schrödinger equation In compact form, Ĥψ = Eψ , where Ĥ is the Hamiltonian (the total-energy operator), ψ is the wavefunction, and E is the energy. Solving it finds the allowed (ψ, E) pairs for a system.

▸ Quantization from boundary conditions For a bound particle, only wavefunctions that "fit" the boundaries are valid — this is what forces energy to be quantized into discrete levels, rather than continuous.

The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle

▸ Uncertainty principle Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2 , where Δx is the uncertainty in position, Δp the uncertainty in momentum, and ℏ = h/2π ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. Shrinking one uncertainty forces the other to grow.

Operators & Observables

▸ Operators and eigenvalues Each observable (energy, momentum, position…) has an operator . When the operator acts on a wavefunction and returns a multiple of it (operator·ψ = a·ψ), the value a is a possible measurement outcome (an eigenvalue), and ψ is an eigenstate.

▸ Expectation value The expectation value ⟨A⟩ is the average result you would get from many measurements on identically prepared systems. It need not be any single allowed value — it is the statistical mean.

📋 Quantum Systems

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

The Particle in a Box

▸ Particle in a box For a particle of mass m confined to a 1-D box of length L, the allowed energies are E_n = n²h² / (8mL²) , with n = 1, 2, 3, …. The wavefunctions are standing waves that must vanish at both walls.

Quantum Tunneling

▸ Quantum tunneling When a particle meets a barrier taller than its energy, its wavefunction does not stop dead — it decays exponentially inside the barrier and emerges with reduced amplitude on the other side. There is a nonzero probability the particle is found beyond the barrier.

The Quantum Harmonic Oscillator

▸ Harmonic oscillator energies E_n = (n + ½)ℏω , with n = 0, 1, 2, …, where ω is the classical angular frequency. The levels are equally spaced by ℏω, and the lowest (n = 0) energy is ½ℏω — the zero-point energy.

The Hydrogen Atom & Quantum Numbers

▸ Hydrogen energy levels As in the Bohr model, the energy depends only on n: E_n = −13.6/n² eV . But the full quantum treatment adds the orbital shapes and orientations that Bohr's simple circles could not capture.

"},"PHYSQ/cheat/c4":{"body":"

📋 Spin & Identical Particles

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Electron Spin & Stern-Gerlach

▸ Spin Spin is a fundamental, built-in angular momentum of a particle, independent of any motion through space. For an electron, the spin quantum number is m_s = +½ or −½ ("spin up" or "spin down") — only two possibilities.

Pauli Exclusion & the Periodic Table

▸ Pauli exclusion principle No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers (n, ℓ, m_ℓ, m_s). Each orbital (a fixed n, ℓ, m_ℓ) therefore holds at most two electrons — one spin up, one spin down.

Bosons & Fermions

▸ Consequences Fermions stacking under Pauli exclusion give atoms their shells and make solid matter rigid. Bosons piling into one state make possible lasers (identical photons), superfluids , and Bose-Einstein condensates .

"},"PHYSQ/cheat/c5":{"body":"

📋 Modern Topics

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Entanglement & Bell's Theorem

▸ Quantum entanglement When two particles are entangled , they form one combined state that cannot be described independently. Measuring one instantly determines the corresponding property of the other, regardless of the distance separating them.

▸ Bell's theorem Bell showed that no theory of "local hidden variables" (pre-determined values carried by each particle) can reproduce quantum predictions. Experiments confirm the quantum correlations, ruling out the comforting classical picture.

Quantum Measurement & Interpretations

▸ Superposition A quantum system can be in a combination of multiple states simultaneously — not "either/or" but "both at once," with each possibility weighted in the wavefunction.

▸ Measurement (collapse) Upon measurement, the system yields a single definite result, and the wavefunction appears to collapse to that outcome. The probability of each result is given by |ψ|².

Introduction to Quantum Computing

▸ Qubit A qubit can be in state 0, state 1, or any superposition of both at once. Only when measured does it yield a definite 0 or 1, with probabilities set by the superposition.

▸ Exponential state space Thanks to superposition, n qubits represent 2ⁿ states simultaneously . Just 300 qubits could encode more states than there are atoms in the observable universe — the source of quantum computing's power.
